newsitem.title: FRANCE: France uses non-tax receipts to balance 96 budget. [CORRECTED 19:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: France uses non-tax receipts to balance 96 budget. [CORRECTED 19:00 GMT]

text.p: The French government on Wednesday approved a revised budget for 1996 which relies on non-tax receipts and spending cuts to fund some 40 billion francs in extra spending, government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said.
The revised budget will maintain the central government budget deficit at 287.9 billion francs ($56.58 billion), just 100 million francs more than the 287.8 billion originally forecast.

It will keep France on course to reduce the total public deficit -- which includes welfare and local authority spending -- to four percent of gross domestic product this year from five percent last year, Lamassoure said.
The total deficit is to be reduced to three percent of GDP next year to meet Maastricht Treaty standards.
Lamassoure said the revised budget covered 40 billion francs in new spending, to be offset by 35 billion francs in savings and six billion in net additional revenues.
The additional revenues come from non-tax receipts, which offset lower-than-expected tax revenues, which were hit by weak economic growth.
The revised budget limited the rise in total spending to 2.2 percent compared to 1995 actual spending. The initial 1996 budget forecast a 1.8 percent rise in spending.

Full details of the revised budget were due to be announced at a news conference by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis at 0700 GMT on Thursday. However, Lamassoure, who is also budget minister, gave the following figures:
SPENDING - The revised budget allows for some 40 billion francs in extra spending, including some 17 billion already decreed in advance and 23 billion in new spending approved in the revised budget.

The new spending includes 4.9 billion in capital injections to state-owned firms, 4.7 billion in housing aid, two billion to fund a government car-buying incentive scheme which expired in September, 1.2 billion for military operations abroad, mainly in Bosnia, and 1.1 billion to fund transfers to state railways SNCF and the RATP, which runs the Paris rail network.

SAVINGS - The revised budget makes total savings of some 35 billion francs, of which 21.5 billion francs will come from scrapping planned spending. A total 6.4 billion will be saved through lower debt service charges due to the fall in interest rates, while 6.8 billion will be saved from the special Treasury accounts. Lamassoure declined to give details on the savings on the special Treasury accounts.
REVENUES - Total revenues are expected to be some six billion francs more than expected.

Revenues from Value Added Tax (sales tax) are expected to be 22 billion francs less than expected, while income tax is seen at 2.17 billion more than expected (corrects from "10 billion less than expected").
This shortfall is to be offset by higher than expected company taxes, for an unspecified amount, and 17 billion francs in additional non-tax receipts.

Lamassoure said these non-tax receipts included a contribution of 3.4 billion francs from state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignation and a contribution of 3.3 billion francs from export credit guarantee agency Coface. He declined to say where the rest of the money would come from.
Charges on revenues are expected to be 8.8 billion francs less than expected, largely due to a reduction in France's contribution to the European Union budget. REUTER
